name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
overview: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common form of skin cancer. It originates from the basal cells of the epidermis and usually develops after years of cumulative ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Although BCC rarely spreads to distant organs, it can progressively invade surrounding skin, cartilage, muscle, and bone if left untreated. Early diagnosis and treatment provide an excellent prognosis.
description: Basal Cell Carcinoma typically develops on chronically sun-exposed areas including the face, nose, ears, scalp, neck, and shoulders. The lesion often grows slowly over months or years and may repeatedly bleed, crust, or ulcerate. Because of its slow progression, patients sometimes mistake it for a non-healing wound. Prompt evaluation is recommended since untreated tumors may cause significant local tissue destruction.
typical_features: Central depression or ulcer in larger lesions

ABCDE.Color: Skin-colored, pink, pearly, brown, or black (pigmented variants)
ABCDE.Evolution: Gradual enlargement, repeated bleeding, or failure to heal should prompt evaluation

risk_factors: Genetic syndromes such as Gorlin syndrome
diagnostic_workup: Additional imaging only if deep tissue invasion is suspected
treatment_options: Mohs micrographic surgery for cosmetically sensitive or high-risk areas
Targeted therapy for selected advanced cases
prognosis: The prognosis is excellent when Basal Cell Carcinoma is diagnosed and treated early. Metastasis is uncommon, but untreated tumors may progressively destroy nearby tissues and require more extensive surgery. Long-term surveillance is recommended because patients who develop one BCC have an increased likelihood of developing additional skin cancers.
prevention: Wear protective clothing, hats, and sunglasses
next_steps: Arrange prompt consultation with a dermatologist.
Histopathological confirmation by biopsy is generally recommended before definitive treatment.
Discuss appropriate treatment options based on lesion size, location, and subtype.
Continue long-term skin surveillance because future skin cancers are more common after one diagnosis.
Protect the affected skin from additional ultraviolet exposure.
red_flags: Loss of sensation around the lesion

follow_up.routine: Dermatology follow-up every 6–12 months depending on recurrence risk and clinician assessment.
follow_up.high_risk: More frequent follow-up may be recommended for recurrent, large, aggressive, or multiple lesions.

patient_advice: Do not ignore lesions that repeatedly bleed or fail to heal.
Take photographs to monitor changes over time.
Protect your skin from future ultraviolet exposure.
Continue regular skin examinations because new lesions may develop even after successful treatment.
